summary.text: For the sequence defined by the candidate linear recurrence, the proof studies the defect \(D_{n+1}=a_{n+1}^2-a_na_{n+2}\); its induced recurrence and growth bounds give \(1\le D_{n+1}\le a_n\). These inequalities force \(\lceil a_{n+1}^2/a_n\rceil-1=a_{n+2}\), so induction identifies the original nonlinear sequence with the linear-recurrence sequence, yielding the claimed generating function.

full_proof.text:
Let \(b_0,b_1,b_2,\ldots\) denote the sequence given by the original definition. Thus
\[
b_0=4,\qquad b_1=16,
\]
and \(b_{n+2}\) is the greatest integer for which
\[
 \frac{b_{n+2}}{b_{n+1}}<\frac{b_{n+1}}{b_n}.
\]
All terms that occur below are positive. After cross-multiplication, the displayed strict inequality says
\[
 b_{n+2}<\frac{b_{n+1}^2}{b_n}.
\]
For any real number \(y\), the greatest integer strictly smaller than \(y\) is \(\lceil y\rceil-1\), including when \(y\) itself is an integer. Consequently, the original rule is equivalently
\[
 b_{n+2}=\left\lceil\frac{b_{n+1}^2}{b_n}\right\rceil-1. \tag{1}
\]
For positive integers this may also be written
\[
 b_{n+2}=\left\lfloor
 \frac{b_{n+1}^2+b_n-1}{b_n}
 \right\rfloor-1. \tag{2}
\]
We will prove that this nonlinear recurrence is satisfied by a sequence with a simple linear recurrence.

Define a sequence \((a_n)_{n\geq 0}\) of nonnegative integers by
\[
a_0=4,\qquad a_1=16,\qquad a_2=63,
\]
and, for every \(n\geq0\),
\[
a_{n+3}=4a_{n+2}-a_n. \tag{3}
\]
Here one may initially regard the subtraction as subtraction in the nonnegative integers; the growth estimate proved next shows that the subtracted quantity is always no larger than the minuend, so (3) is also an ordinary integer equality. Its first few terms are
\[
4,16,63,248,976,3841,\ldots.
\]

We first establish the growth estimate
\[
a_{n+1}\geq 3a_n\quad\hbox{and}\quad a_n>0 \qquad(n\geq0). \tag{4}
\]
The first three instances are immediate:
\[
16\geq3\cdot4,\qquad 63\geq3\cdot16,\qquad
248=4\cdot63-4\geq3\cdot63.
\]
Suppose inductively that the estimates needed at earlier indices have been established. In particular,
\[
a_{n+3}\geq3a_{n+2},\qquad a_{n+2}\geq3a_{n+1},
\]
so \(a_{n+3}\geq a_{n+1}\). By the defining recurrence,
\[
a_{n+4}=4a_{n+3}-a_{n+1}\geq3a_{n+3}>0.
\]
This proves (4) by strong induction. It also confirms that all the subtractions in (3) are ordinary subtractions. In particular, we may freely use the equivalent identity
\[
a_{n+3}+a_n=4a_{n+2}. \tag{5}
\]

The crucial point is to control how far the middle square \(a_{n+1}^2\) lies above the product \(a_na_{n+2}\). To do so, introduce an auxiliary integer sequence \((D_n)_{n\geq0}\) by
\[
D_0=0,\qquad D_1=4,\qquad D_2=1,\qquad D_3=16,
\]
and
\[
D_{n+4}=4D_{n+2}+D_{n+1}\qquad(n\geq0). \tag{6}
\]
We claim that
\[
a_{n+1}^2=a_na_{n+2}+D_{n+1} \qquad(n\geq0). \tag{7}
\]
For \(n=0,1,2\), this follows from the direct calculations
\[
16^2=4\cdot63+4,
\]
\[
63^2=16\cdot248+1,
\]
and
\[
248^2=63\cdot976+16.
\]

For the induction step, it is useful to write, in ordinary integer arithmetic,
\[
E_n=a_{n+1}^2-a_na_{n+2}.
\]
We show directly from (5) that
\[
E_{n+3}=4E_{n+1}+E_n. \tag{8}
\]
Indeed, using
\[
a_{n+5}=4a_{n+4}-a_{n+2}
\quad\hbox{and}\quad
a_{n+4}=4a_{n+3}-a_{n+1},
\]
we obtain
\[
\begin{aligned}
E_{n+3}
 &=a_{n+4}^2-a_{n+3}a_{n+5}\\
 &=a_{n+4}^2-a_{n+3}(4a_{n+4}-a_{n+2})\\
 &=a_{n+4}(a_{n+4}-4a_{n+3})+a_{n+2}a_{n+3}\\
 &=-a_{n+1}a_{n+4}+a_{n+2}a_{n+3}\\
 &=-a_{n+1}(4a_{n+3}-a_{n+1})+a_{n+2}a_{n+3}. \tag{9}
\end{aligned}
\]
On the other hand, since \(a_n=4a_{n+2}-a_{n+3}\),
\[
\begin{aligned}
4E_{n+1}+E_n
 &=4(a_{n+2}^2-a_{n+1}a_{n+3})
   +(a_{n+1}^2-a_na_{n+2})\\
 &=4a_{n+2}^2-4a_{n+1}a_{n+3}+a_{n+1}^2
   -(4a_{n+2}-a_{n+3})a_{n+2}\\
 &=-4a_{n+1}a_{n+3}+a_{n+1}^2+a_{n+2}a_{n+3},
\end{aligned}
\]
which is exactly the last expression in (9). Thus (8) holds.

Now suppose (7) is known at indices \(n\) and \(n+1\). Then (8) and the recurrence (6) give
\[
E_{n+3}=4E_{n+1}+E_n
       =4D_{n+2}+D_{n+1}
       =D_{n+4}.
\]
Together with the three initial cases, strong induction proves (7) for every \(n\).

We next need two bounds on this defect:
\[
1\leq D_{n+1}\leq a_n \qquad(n\geq0). \tag{10}
\]

First, positivity is immediate in the initial cases:
\[
D_1=4,\qquad D_2=1,\qquad D_3=16.
\]
For every later term, (6) expresses \(D_{n+4}\) as
\[
D_{n+4}=4D_{n+2}+D_{n+1}.
\]
In particular, once the preceding relevant terms are positive, this term is positive as well. Strong induction therefore gives \(D_{n+1}\geq1\) for all \(n\).

For the upper bound, the first three cases are again direct:
\[
D_1=4\leq a_0=4,
\quad D_2=1\leq a_1=16,
\quad D_3=16\leq a_2=63.
\]
Suppose the desired upper bounds have already been established at earlier indices. For an index of the form \(n=m+3\), recurrence (6) and the induction hypotheses give
\[
D_{m+4}=4D_{m+2}+D_{m+1}
       \leq4a_{m+1}+a_m. \tag{11}
\]
We compare the right side with \(a_{m+3}\). From (3),
\[
a_{m+3}=4a_{m+2}-a_m.
\]
The growth estimate (4) gives
\[
a_{m+2}\geq3a_{m+1},\qquad a_{m+1}\geq3a_m.
\]
In particular,
\[
4a_{m+2}-a_m\geq 12a_{m+1}-a_m
                    \geq4a_{m+1}+a_m.
\]
(The final inequality only requires \(8a_{m+1}\geq2a_m\), which follows at once from \(a_{m+1}\geq3a_m\).) Combining this with (11) yields
\[
D_{m+4}\leq a_{m+3}.
\]
Thus the upper bound, and hence all of (10), follows by strong induction.

We can now evaluate the nonlinear ceiling recurrence exactly. By (7),
\[
a_{n+1}^2=a_na_{n+2}+D_{n+1}.
\]
Adding \(a_n-1\) to both sides gives
\[
a_{n+1}^2+a_n-1
 =a_n(a_{n+2}+1)+(D_{n+1}-1). \tag{12}
\]
By (10),
\[
0\leq D_{n+1}-1<a_n.
\]
Therefore (12) is precisely the quotient-and-remainder decomposition upon division by \(a_n\), and consequently
\[
\left\lfloor
\frac{a_{n+1}^2+a_n-1}{a_n}
\right\rfloor=a_{n+2}+1.
\]
Subtracting one gives
\[
a_{n+2}
 =\left\lfloor
\frac{a_{n+1}^2+a_n-1}{a_n}
\right\rfloor-1
 =\left\lceil\frac{a_{n+1}^2}{a_n}\right\rceil-1. \tag{13}
\]
Thus \((a_n)\) obeys exactly the original extremal rule.

For completeness, we now identify the two sequences by induction rather than merely appealing to uniqueness informally. At indices \(0\) and \(1\), both sequences have values \(4\) and \(16\). Suppose \(b_n=a_n\) and \(b_{n+1}=a_{n+1}\). Applying the original recurrence (1), then the induction hypotheses, and finally (13), gives
\[
\begin{aligned}
b_{n+2}
 &=\left\lceil\frac{b_{n+1}^2}{b_n}\right\rceil-1\\
 &=\left\lceil\frac{a_{n+1}^2}{a_n}\right\rceil-1\\
 &=a_{n+2}.
\end{aligned}
\]
Hence
\[
b_n=a_n\qquad\text{for every }n\geq0. \tag{14}
\]
In particular,
\[
b_0=4,\qquad b_1=16,
\]
and
\[
b_2=\left\lceil\frac{16^2}{4}\right\rceil-1=64-1=63.
\]
Using (3) and (14), for every \(n\geq3\) we have
\[
\boxed{\ b_n=4b_{n-1}-b_{n-3}\ }. \tag{15}
\]
This is the claimed linear recurrence for the original-definition variant.

It remains to translate (15) into the stated generating function. Let
\[
B(x)=\sum_{n\geq0}b_nx^n
\]
be the ordinary generating function, interpreted as a formal power series. The coefficient of \(x^n\) in
\[
(1-4x+x^3)B(x)
\]
is \(b_n-4b_{n-1}+b_{n-3}\), with terms having negative indices omitted. For \(n\geq3\), this coefficient is zero by (15). The coefficients in degrees \(0,1,2\) are respectively
\[
b_0=4,
\]
\[
b_1-4b_0=16-16=0,
\]
and
\[
b_2-4b_1=63-64=-1.
\]
Therefore
\[
(1-4x+x^3)B(x)=4-x^2.
\]
Since the denominator has constant term \(1\), it is invertible as a formal power series, and hence
\[
\boxed{
B(x)=\frac{4-x^2}{1-4x+x^3}
}.
\]
This proves the conjectured generating function for the sequence arising from the original, always-greatest-integer definition.
